tools.name: -health-check
tools.description: Internal health check tool. Verifies WebSocket connectivity to the backend terminal API.

tools.name: terminal-create
tools.description: Open a terminal session in the workspace's Linux machine (the same workspace files and tools as the Bash app). It is a shared terminal: it runs in the workspace's machine with the workspace's home, never in a person's personal terminal. It is yours: its "Agent" switch is on, and the workspace's members can see it, each session in its own Terminal window (show, default true, opens or focuses that window for the user); to type in it they switch it to "Agent off". With agent="claude" (or "codex", "opencode") the session starts that coding agent (installing it on first use) and waits until it is ready for a prompt — then use terminal-prompt. Claude Code runs on the API key of the workspace owner's Anthropic provider in Teros; with none it shows its login screen: stop and tell the user (Teros never asks for, stores or shares a Claude sign-in). Without agent you get a bash shell — use terminal-run for commands. Each call opens a NEW session: check terminal-list first and reuse yours. Sessions are kept until terminal-destroy: idle ones sleep and wake (same directory while it still exists, Claude Code on its conversation) the next time a tool uses them.

agent.description: Start a coding agent in the session: "claude" (Claude Code), "codex" or "opencode". The call returns once it is ready for a prompt (or says what it waits for).

cwd.description: Working directory (default /workspace). For a shell, verified: cwdApplied tells whether the cd worked and cwdError carries the shell error (e.g. "No such file or directory").

title.description: Short label the user sees on the window and in the "Sessions" list — set one (e.g. "deploy logs", "fix login bug")

show.description: Open or focus this session's Terminal window in the user's app so they can watch (default: true)

annotations.summary: Open a terminal session (a shell, or Claude Code / Codex / opencode)

tools.name: terminal-prompt
tools.description: Send a prompt to the coding agent running in a session (Claude Code, Codex, opencode) and wait until its turn ends: it finished (done), asks something / wants a permission (blocked), shows its login screen, or left. Returns what happened and the screen with its answer. Multi-line prompts are pasted as one message. If it is still working when the wait runs out, call terminal-wait until="turn" — never send the prompt again. Also use it for slash commands ("/clear", "/exit") and to answer a free-text question.

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait for the turn to end (default 90000, max 100000)

annotations.summary: Give a coding agent (Claude Code…) a prompt and wait for its turn to end

tools.name: terminal-wait
tools.description: Wait for something to happen in a session instead of sleeping or polling, then get the screen. until: "turn" — the coding agent finished its turn, asks something, shows its login screen or left (after terminal-prompt / terminal-send-key); "ready" — a coding agent started and waits for a prompt; "exit" — the running shell command finished; "quiet" — no output for quietMs (any program settled); "text" — the screen shows `text` (case-insensitive) or matches the regex `pattern`. Only what happens after your last write/prompt/key counts. A timeout is not an error: it says what is going on, and you can call it again. If a person switches the session to "Agent off" or starts typing in it, the wait stops early (reason "driver"): don't type until control is yours again — a note they leave when switching "Agent" on comes with your next wait/read (handedBack).

until.description: What to wait for (see the tool description)

text.description: until="text": text the screen must show

pattern.description: until="text": JavaScript regex matched against the whole screen

quietMs.description: until="quiet": how long without output counts as settled (default 1500)

timeoutMs.description: Give up after this many ms (default 30000, max 100000)

annotations.summary: Wait for a coding agent's turn, a ready prompt, quiet output, text, or exit

tools.name: terminal-run
tools.description: Run a command line in a shell session, wait for it to finish (up to timeoutMs) and return its output. The user sees it run in that session's Terminal window. For long or interactive programs it returns what they printed so far and that they are still running: then use terminal-wait until="exit", terminal-screen, terminal-send-key (ctrl-c to stop). For a coding agent use terminal-prompt instead.

command.description: The command line (newlines run several lines)

timeoutMs.description: How long to wait for it to finish (default 30000, max 100000)

annotations.summary: Run a shell command in a session and get its output

tools.name: terminal-screen
tools.description: The rendered screen of a session as plain text, as a person looking at it sees it, plus what runs in it and the coding agent's state. Use it for full-screen programs (Claude Code, vim, htop, menus, installers). onlyChanges returns just the rows that changed since your last look (row numbers from 0).

onlyChanges.description: Only the rows that changed since the last screen you got (default false)

annotations.summary: Look at the terminal screen as the user sees it

tools.name: terminal-read
tools.description: Read the output log of a session (escape codes removed): the last `lines` lines (default 200) or, with `since`, only what came after that cursor — every answer ends with the cursor to pass next time. Good for logs and command output; for full-screen programs (Claude Code, vim) use terminal-screen instead, the log of a TUI is redraw fragments.

lines.description: Return at most this many trailing lines (default: 200)

since.description: Cursor from a previous read/run/wait-for: only output after it

annotations.summary: Read a session's output log (plain text, incremental)

tools.name: terminal-write
tools.description: Type text into a session, then press Enter (sendEnter, default true). Low-level: prefer terminal-run for shell commands and terminal-prompt for coding agents, which also wait for the result. Multi-line text goes in as one paste when the program supports it. Use sendEnter false to fill an input without submitting it.

sendEnter.description: Press Enter after the text (default: true)

annotations.summary: Type text into a terminal session

tools.name: terminal-send-key
tools.description: Press one key or a sequence of keys in a session: pick menu options (keys ["down","enter"]), answer a permission prompt ("1", "enter"), interrupt (ctrl-c), leave (ctrl-d), cancel (escape), cycle modes (shift-tab). Keys: enter, tab, shift-tab, escape, backspace, delete, space, up, down, left, right, home, end, pageup, pagedown, insert, f1–f12, ctrl-<letter> (ctrl-c, ctrl-d, ctrl-r…), alt-<key> (alt-b, alt-enter…), or a single character. Then terminal-wait to see the effect.

keys.description: Several keys pressed in order, e.g. ["down","down","enter"]

annotations.summary: Press keys in a terminal session (enter, arrows, ctrl-c, escape…)

tools.name: terminal-wait-for
tools.description: Wait until a line of the session's output log matches a JavaScript regex (checked against what is buffered, then every new line). By default only output after your last terminal-write counts, so the echo of the command itself never matches. For screens of full-screen programs and coding agents use terminal-wait (until="text" / "turn").

pattern.description: JavaScript regex to match against output lines (e.g. "\$ $", "password:", "done")

timeoutMs.description: Give up after this many ms (default: 10000, max: 100000)

since.description: Only consider output at or after this cursor (from read/run/wait-for)

annotations.summary: Wait until a session's output log matches a regex

tools.name: terminal-list
tools.description: List the terminal sessions you can reach in this workspace: the ones agents opened (the workspace's members see those too) and the ones a person opened and switched to "Agent". A session a person opens, their personal terminal or a shared one, is not listed while it reads "Agent off": to work in it, ask them to switch it to "Agent" in that session's Terminal window. Each line has the id, title, what runs in it, the coding agent's state (working / blocked = waiting for someone / done), which space it is in (a person's personal terminal, or a shared one in the workspace's machine), who opened it, who is typing, who is watching, and whether it is asleep (idle sessions freeze, then sleep; any tool that uses one wakes it). Reuse a session instead of opening a new one.

annotations.summary: List the terminal sessions you can reach

tools.name: terminal-request-control
tools.description: Ask for control of a session you can reach while a person is typing in it (your writes there are refused with "<name> is typing in this session" until they have typed nothing for 60 s). The person gets "Allow" / "Keep off" in this chat and in that session's Terminal window; "Allow" switches it to "Agent" for you at once. Waits up to 90 s: granted (nobody was typing), approved (you may type), denied (don't type; say in chat what you need or open your own session), pending (call again to keep waiting) or busy (another agent asked first; nothing was sent). It cannot reach a person's own session that reads "Agent off": only they switch that on.

reason.description: What you want to do there, in a few words (e.g. "run the tests")

annotations.summary: Ask the person for control of a session

tools.name: terminal-release-control
tools.description: Let go of a session you are typing in, when the person asks you to stop, let them type or give them control. Then tell them how: they switch it to "Agent off" in that session's Terminal window and type (while an agent types, a person's keys are not sent). Don't type there again until they switch it back to "Agent" (a note they leave comes with your next call) or you ask with terminal-request-control. Answers released, or who is typing when it wasn't you (nothing changes).

annotations.summary: Let go of control of a session

tools.name: terminal-show
tools.description: Open or focus a session's own Terminal window in the user's app (one window shows one session), so they can watch what happens in it. terminal-create already does this unless show=false.

annotations.summary: Open a session's Terminal window for the user

tools.name: terminal-destroy
tools.description: End a session and kill whatever runs in it (what "End session" in the window's ⋯ menu does; closing a window never ends its session). Only end sessions you opened, or that the user asked you to end.
